name: Irish
variety: Traditional Gaeltacht Irish. There is no single spoken standard: the inventory follows Ní Chasaide (1999) and Ó Siadhail (1989), and Munster (West Kerry) values are given where dialects differ, because the rules of eSpeak NG are built on Munster pronunciation.
sources: Ní Chasaide, Ailbhe (1999). Irish. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association. Cambridge University Press, 111-116.
Ó Siadhail, Mícheál (1989). Modern Irish: Grammatical Structure and Dialectal Variation. Cambridge University Press.
Ó Sé, Diarmuid (2000). Gaeilge Chorca Dhuibhne. Dublin: Institiúid Teangeolaíochta Éireann.
Ó Cuív, Brian (1944). The Irish of West Muskerry, Co. Cork. Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies.
de Bhaldraithe, Tomás (1945). The Irish of Cois Fhairrge, Co. Galway. Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies.
Hickey, Raymond (2014). The Sound Structure of Modern Irish. De Gruyter Mouton.
Ní Chiosáin, Máire; Padgett, Jaye (2012). An acoustic and perceptual study of Connemara Irish palatalization. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(2): 171-191.

Bennett, Ryan; Ní Chiosáin, Máire; Padgett, Jaye; McGuire, Grant (2018). An ultrasound study of Connemara Irish palatalization and velarization. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 48(3): 261-304.
Dalton, Martha; Ní Chasaide, Ailbhe (2005). Tonal alignment in Irish dialects. Language and Speech 48(4): 441-464.
contrasts: every consonant except /h/ comes in a broad (velarised) and a slender (palatalised) form; the contrast carries lexical and grammatical meaning (bó 'cow' against beo 'alive'; bád 'boat' against báid 'boats')
for velars the pair is velar against palatal: /k ɡ x ɣ ŋ/ against /c ɟ ç j ɲ/; for /sˠ/ the slender partner is postalveolar /ʃ/
vowel length: five short vowels, five long vowels, and schwa in unstressed syllables
tense against lax sonorants (written nn, ll, rr against n, l, r) in Connacht and Ulster, largely given up in Munster
voicing in stops; voiceless stops are aspirated
initial mutations (lenition and eclipsis) change the first consonant of a word by grammatical rule
allophony: a broad consonant before a front vowel has a velar off-glide [ɰ] (buí, naoi), and a slender consonant before a back vowel has a palatal off-glide [j] (beo, ciúin); matching on-glides occur after vowels
broad coronals /t̪ˠ d̪ˠ n̪ˠ l̪ˠ/ are dental; slender /tʲ dʲ/ are palatalised alveolar or alveolo-palatal stops in Munster and affricates [t͡ɕ d͡ʑ] in Ulster and parts of Connacht
vowel quality follows the neighbouring consonants: vowels are fronted between slender and retracted between broad consonants
unstressed short vowels are reduced to [ə], or to [ɪ] next to a slender consonant
an unwritten vowel [ə] is inserted between /l n r/ and a following labial or velar consonant after a short stressed vowel (gorm, ainm, dearg)
short vowels are lengthened or made diphthongs before tense sonorants at the end of a word or before a consonant, by dialect: ceann is [caun̪ˠ] in Munster, [cɑːn̪ˠ] in Connacht and [can̪ˠ] in Ulster
a voiced obstruent next to /h/ is devoiced
vowels are nasalised next to nasal consonants
phonotactics: the consonants of a cluster agree in quality: all broad or all slender; the spelling shows the quality by the neighbouring vowel letters
initial clusters of up to three consonants (str, spr, scr); further clusters arise from mutation (mb, gc, bhf are spellings of single sounds)
/x ɣ ŋ/ and slender /ç ɲ/ begin a word only through mutation
long vowels and diphthongs occur in unstressed syllables, mostly in Munster and Connacht

stress.type: fixed initial in Connacht and Ulster; weight-sensitive in Munster
stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable; in Munster a long vowel or diphthong in the second or third syllable takes the stress (cailín, amadán), as does -ach in the second syllable after a short first syllable (bacach).
stress.cues: pitch movement, duration and full vowel quality; unstressed short vowels are reduced to schwa, and in Ulster unstressed long vowels are shortened

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed short vowels become [ə] or [ɪ]

length.notes: Long vowels are written with an acute accent. No figures for the long to short ratio are given here because none could be checked. The old tense sonorants were long; today they differ from the lax ones in place and secondary articulation, where the contrast survives.

intonation.declarative: Connacht and Munster: falling accents (H*+L) on stressed syllables, each peak lower than the last, with a final fall. Ulster (Donegal): rising accents (L*+H), the last one included, so that statements typically end on a rise or a high plateau.
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the particle an; the tune is the same as in a statement, falling in Connacht and Munster and rising in Ulster, with higher pitch peaks
intonation.wh_question: falling in Connacht and Munster, with the peak on the question word
intonation.continuation: level pitch or a small rise at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: H*+L in Connacht and Munster: peak in the stressed syllable, then a fall; L*+H in Ulster: low in the stressed syllable, rising into the next

problems: slender consonants are made by adding a separate [j] glide to a plain consonant, and only before certain vowel spellings; at the end of a word or before a consonant they often come out plain or broad (the final consonants of bliain, cailín, ainm and boird)
broad consonants are not velarised; before front vowels the broad quality is imitated by an inserted [w] or schwa, which adds a syllable (naoi as [nəˈiː], gaoth as [ɡəˈeː], buí as [bwiː])
broad r is the English approximant [ɹ]; slender r is a trill, or [ʒ] between vowels (Éire); Irish has taps
slender d is the affricate [d͡ʒ] but slender t is a palatal stop [c] or [t͡ʃ], a mixture of dialect values

dialects are mixed: vowel rules are Munster-like (ceann with [au], ao as [eː], final -igh with [ɡ]) but stress stays on the first syllable, with at most a secondary stress on a later long vowel (bradán, amadán; none in cailín)
broad and slender l and n differ only by the added glide; there are no dental or velarised laterals and nasals and no tense sonorants
words containing the letters j, k, q, w, x, y, z are handed to the English voice
IPA output prints the back vowel phoneme '0' as the letter A
intonation is generic and not based on any Irish dialect
good: lenition and eclipsis spellings are read correctly (bhf, mb, gc, nd, dt, bp, ts; ch, gh, dh, th, sh, fh)
the inserted vowel in gorm, ainm, dearg
long and short vowels, and schwa in unstressed syllables
broad t and d are dental
slender s is [ʃ], and ch, gh, dh have velar and palatal values

notes: A synthesiser needs the broad and slender series as consonant qualities with their glides, not as consonant plus vowel sequences. Vowel formants and VOT are left out because no figures could be checked; formant targets for vowels must in any case depend on the quality of the neighbouring consonants.
